chapters.title: Chapter 2: Measuring Trend - Moving Averages and Crossovers

lessons.title: Simple vs Exponential Moving Averages: Mechanics and When to Use Each

children.text: Every trend-following system, from a simple retail crossover strategy to an institutional CTA's futures book, needs a way to answer one basic question: is this asset trending up or down right now? The most common answer, by far, is the moving average, a running average of recent prices that smooths out day-to-day noise and reveals the underlying direction. This lesson covers the two moving averages you will use throughout this course, the simple moving average and the exponential moving average, how each is actually calculated, and why the choice between them is not just a technical footnote.

body.text: A moving average is a smoothed version of a price series, recalculated at every new data point using only the most recent window of prices. It exists to filter out short-term noise so a trader can see the underlying trend, at the cost of reacting to changes in that trend with some delay.

markDefs.definition: The unweighted average of a security's closing price over the most recent n periods, recalculated as each new period's close becomes available.

children.text: gives every price in its look-back window equal weight. A 5-day SMA is just the average of the last 5 closing prices, recalculated fresh each day as the oldest price drops out and the newest one is added.

body.caption: The n-period SMA at time t: the unweighted average of the n most recent closing prices, P_t being the most recent.

markDefs.definition: A moving average that weights recent prices more heavily than older ones, using a smoothing constant, so it reacts to new price changes faster than a simple moving average of the same length.

children.text: weights recent prices more heavily than older ones, with the weight decaying exponentially the further back in time you go. Rather than recomputing a full average over a window each period, it is calculated recursively: today's EMA is a blend of today's price and yesterday's EMA value.

body.caption: The n-period EMA: a weighted blend of today's price and yesterday's EMA value. The smoothing constant alpha determines how much weight today's price gets, larger n means smaller alpha and slower reaction.

children.text: For a 5-day EMA, alpha works out to 2 / (5 + 1) = 0.333, meaning today's price gets roughly a third of the weight and the prior EMA value carries the rest, which itself embeds a decaying memory of every price before it. A common convention, used in the worked example below, is to seed the very first EMA value with the SMA of the first n periods, since there is no prior EMA value to build on at the very start of a series.
Worked Example: SMA and EMA on the Same Ten Days

Take ten illustrative daily closing prices for a hypothetical NSE-listed stock: 100, 102, 101, 104, 106, 105, 108, 110, 109, 112. Both a 5-day SMA and a 5-day EMA need at least 5 days of data before the first value can be calculated.

body.caption: 5-day SMA and 5-day EMA on illustrative closing prices (rounded to 2 decimals)

body.text: By Day 10, the SMA reads 108.80 while the EMA reads 108.94. The EMA is slightly higher because it gives the recent jump to 112 more weight than the SMA does, the SMA still carries equal weight from Day 6's 105, five days back. This is the practical difference between the two: the EMA moves faster to reflect what has just happened.

body.title: SMA vs EMA on the same illustrative price series

body.caption: Computing both moving averages in pandas
body.code:
import pandas as pd

close = pd.Series([100, 102, 101, 104, 106, 105, 108, 110, 109, 112])

sma_5 = close.rolling(window=5).mean()
ema_5 = close.ewm(span=5, adjust=False).mean()

result = pd.DataFrame({"close": close, "sma_5": sma_5, "ema_5": ema_5})
print(result)

body.text: pandas' ewm(adjust=False) seeds the very first EMA value with the first closing price itself, not the SMA of the first n periods used in the hand-calculated example above. This means the two approaches produce slightly different EMA values in the first few periods after the series starts, though they converge closely as more data accumulates. Know which convention your tools use before comparing EMA values across systems.

children.text: The SMA's equal weighting makes it smoother and less prone to whipsaws, false signals from short-lived price spikes, which is why the 50-day and 200-day SMA are the industry-standard convention for defining a long-term trend on an index like the Nifty 50 or on a large, liquid stock. The tradeoff is lag: because old prices matter just as much as new ones until they fall out of the window, the SMA reacts slowly to a genuine change in trend. The EMA's extra weight on recent prices makes it more responsive, useful for shorter, faster systems, including the 12-day and 26-day EMAs that feed into the MACD indicator, and for tracking more volatile NSE midcap and smallcap stocks where a slow-reacting SMA can mean giving back a large chunk of a move before the signal catches up. The tradeoff runs the other way: an EMA's extra sensitivity also means more false signals in a genuinely choppy, sideways market. Neither version is objectively better, the choice depends on how much lag you are willing to accept in exchange for fewer false signals, a tradeoff this course returns to directly when building crossover systems next.

columns.label: Simple Moving Average
points: Equal weight on every price in the window
Smoother, fewer false signals from short spikes
Reacts to a genuine trend change more slowly

columns.label: Exponential Moving Average
points: More weight on recent prices, decaying for older ones
Reacts to a genuine trend change faster
More prone to false signals in choppy markets

body.title: Calculate a 3-day SMA by hand
body.prompt: A stock closes at 50, 52, and 54 on three consecutive days. What is the 3-day SMA on the third day?
body.explanation: (50 + 52 + 54) / 3 = 156 / 3 = 52. With only three data points and an equal-weighted average, the SMA on the third day is simply the arithmetic mean of all three closes.

body.title: SMA or EMA?
body.question: A stock has been flat for months, then jumps sharply on a strong earnings result and keeps climbing for the next two weeks. Which moving average, a 20-day SMA or a 20-day EMA of the same length, will start reflecting the new uptrend sooner?
options: The 20-day SMA, because it uses more historical data
The 20-day EMA, because it weights the recent, post-earnings prices more heavily
Both will react at exactly the same speed
Neither will react, moving averages only work on indices, not individual stocks
body.explanation: The EMA's exponential weighting gives recent prices, including the sharp post-earnings move, more influence than the SMA's equal weighting does, so it turns upward and reflects the new trend sooner.

body.label: Plot SMA and EMA overlays on Zerodha Kite or TradingView
body.description: Both Zerodha's Kite charting tool and TradingView let you overlay multiple SMA and EMA lines of different lengths directly on a live NSE or BSE chart, the fastest way to build intuition for how each one behaves.

cards.definition: The unweighted average of a security's closing price over the most recent n periods.
A moving average that weights recent prices more heavily than older ones using a smoothing constant, reacting faster than an SMA of the same length.
In an EMA, the weight given to the most recent price, calculated as 2 divided by (n + 1) for an n-period EMA.
The delay between a genuine change in an asset's trend and a moving average reflecting that change, larger for longer windows and for the SMA relative to the EMA.
A false trend signal caused by short-term price noise rather than a genuine change in direction, more common with faster, more reactive indicators.

points: A moving average smooths a price series to reveal the underlying trend, at the cost of reacting to genuine trend changes with some delay.
The SMA weights every price in its window equally, making it smoother but slower to react. The EMA weights recent prices more heavily, making it faster to react but more prone to whipsaws.
The 50-day and 200-day SMA are the industry-standard convention for reading long-term trend on indices like the Nifty 50 and on large, liquid stocks.
The EMA's speed makes it useful for shorter, faster systems, including the 12-day and 26-day EMAs behind the MACD indicator, and for more volatile midcap and smallcap names.

Different tools can seed the first EMA value differently, hand calculations often use the SMA of the first n periods, while pandas' default uses the first price. Know which convention you are using before comparing values.
